data.name: SiN Gold (1998)
data.detailed_description:
When the CEO of SinTEK Industries begins injecting the streets with a DNA-altering drug, it's time to reassess the laws of morality. When the same twisted bio-chemist plans to overtake the world with her unholy army of genetically-engineered mutants, it's time to rewrite the golden rule.





You are Colonel John R. Blade, head of the most prominent private protection agency in Freeport. Now Elexis Sinclaire is waging her holy war against the security industry...and you along with it. You've made a religion out of fighting crime. Now you're going to make Elexis pay for her sins.





Updated Features
* Added "Wages of SiN" expansion
* Added modernized Steam master server support
* Added and restored editing SDK
* Added support for additional 16:9 video resolutions
* Restored/uncensored various original game assets

General Improvements
* Optimizations to math, container types, and search algorithms
* Restored support for *.sin pack files, re-packed assets
* Removed obsolete IPX networking support
* Restored original sound and music engine
* Changed video format to open-source/patent-free OGV/Theora

Fixes
* Fixed crash in Docks cinematic
* Fixed incorrect behavior in Thug AI
* Fixed undefined camera position and occasional crash in Wages of SiN ending cinematic
* r_palettemode cvar for software mode now reads and writes correct configuration variable
* Fixed memory corruption issue during multiplayer initialization
* cl_maxfps default changed to 200 to avoid issues with game running too fast
* Repaired issue with extremely loud sounds on menu screens when FPS is too high
* Fixed possible soft lock when using menu hotkeys while inside an in-game computer console
* Restored missing assets for Beecadrone enemy

reviews.review:
With the remaster finally launching I guess I'd better finally leave some thoughts on the OG version. [i]SiN[/i] is one of those games I always expect to be a little worse than it is, but then I play it and realize "Wait this is awesome" but then I get to one of the more gimmicky levels that tries something that doesn't quite work and I go "man I wish this was over" only to go back to one of the good levels and be right back into it all over again.

I've played through this release twice, one being the first steam release which just had the base game and was censored. Around 2020 they did kind of a "Half-Remaster" that got the game more stable, fixed a few bugs, uncensored a few things, and biggest of all added the [i]Wages of SiN[/i] expansion pack (which I do still need to play). I started a playthrough when that came out and in the past few days I realized I never finished it so I took the past few days to finish the final few levels.

The downside is while they did touch it up to run well, it's not hte most friendly to higher resolution screens. If you play on anything higher than 1080p the UI will basically be the size of your fingernail tucked away in the corner of the screen, though the game itself is still basically playable. There's a source port called Dominatrix you can install that apparently lets you scale the UI so if you're gonna play this version of [i]SiN[/i] that might be the play though I've heard it can break some of the rope climbing mechanics in the expansion so it's not a perfect option. I imagine SiN Reloaded will be the way to go for technical aspects but this is still here if you want the [i]most[/i] original experience (also for some reason after I closed out my latest session of the game it re-enabled mouse acceleration in my windows settings so make of that what you will. I think maybe because the game crashed and games tend to un-set it that option on a proper close).

Jank aside, the game itself is, I think, the truest successor to [i]Duke Nukem 3D[/i]. Not just because one of the level designers from that game was the lead designer on this (Rich "Levelord" Gray), l but the whole philosophy of the level design. The levels are full of weird little knick-knacks to mess with, if you press a button something cool will probably happen and exploration is always [i]deeply[/i] rewarded. There's always [i]something[/i] around every corner if you look and sometimes you'll even stumble into a whole alternate level, a new path, or something you do in one level will affect something that happens in another level. In some ways it kind of feels like if one of those insane notorious feature creep games like [i]Duke Forever[/i] or whatever Peter Molyneux's latest zany scheme is actually shipped on time and mostly delivered on its promises. There's cool stuff like in-game PC's with command lines that actually work with DOS commands like DIR and CD. The weapons themselves are a ton of fun and feel great to use and John Blade is one of the great underrated protagonists of 90's shooters. On the surface he's a bit like Duke and even has some of the same one-liners but there's kind of this unspoken but intentional thread that he's not [i]quite[/i] as cool as he seems, like a more competent Jack Burton. Some of his one-liners are less "tough" and more "He couldn't come up with something clever on the spot so he said something totally whack" and that humanizes him in a way you don't get from your typical 90's tough guy protagonists. For all the issues [i]Phantom Fury[/i] had I think it is telling that Blade has at least stayed in the conversation long enough to have a cameo in that game, he's just got a certain charming "something" that makes him lovable.

That said it's not a perfect game and you can kind of see why it lost out to [i]Half-Life[/i]. I think it's a much closer battle than some made it out to be but the Day 1 release was also pretty buggy from what I understand. Some levels have a gimmick like riding a motorcycle or something, and while it's impressive that it's there [i]at all[/i] the vehicle controls are [i]exceptionally twitchy[/i]. Some levels will take away your weapons and force you into a long stealth sequence that doesn't work well, some stretches of the game just feel [i]long[/i]/ Like I get wanting quantity but this game has a [i]lot[/i] of levels and whenever it feels like you're nearing the climax chances are [i]you probably aren't[/i].

Still, there's a lot to like, some of it almost feels like a proto [i]Deus-Ex[/i] immersive sim, especially when they let you disable security systems, and it genuinely feels like you have some degree of freedom in how to approach solving things. There's no "wrong" path to take and you won't see everything on the first playthrough.

Visually the maps and models look quite good for their time, particularly the lighting and weapons. Since this is a Quake II engine game your hands and basically every character wobbles around like Jell-O because of the loose way it handles floating point math but it's part of the charm and I dare say this game is a far more interesting use of the Quake II engine than... the actual Quake II.

Whether this particular version of the game retains any merit compared to Reloaded remains to be seen but if you've already got it and just want to play the game it's still an option.
